title: Resources
text:
Getting started

R from CRAN

Download and install R itself, for Windows, macOS or Linux.

RStudio Desktop or Positron

Editors that make writing R code much easier. Install R first.

Posit Cloud

Run R in your web browser, with nothing to install.

Your first steps in R

Our own 30-minute tutorial for complete beginners.

swirl

Learn R interactively, inside R itself.

title: Resources
text:
Free online books

R for Data Science (2nd edition)

The standard introduction to importing, cleaning, exploring and visualising data with the tidyverse.

Hands-On Programming with R

Learn to program in R through small, practical projects.

The Epidemiologist R Handbook

A practical reference for public health and epidemiology work, written by and for field epidemiologists.

ggplot2: Elegant Graphics for Data Analysis

Everything you need to make clear, beautiful charts.

Geocomputation with R

Working with maps and spatial data.

Tidy Modeling with R

Statistical modelling and machine learning with the tidymodels packages.

Mastering Shiny

Build interactive web apps and dashboards in R.

Advanced R and R Packages

For when you’re ready to go deeper and share your own code.

Big Book of R

A searchable collection of hundreds of free R books, sorted by topic.

title: Resources
text:
Courses and lessons

Data Carpentry

Free, community-written lessons that teach data skills to researchers, with several R lessons.

Quarto

Create reports, slides and websites (like this one) from your R code.

title: Resources
text:
Tanzanian and regional data
Practise with data about the places and questions you care about.

National Bureau of Statistics (NBS)

Official Tanzanian statistics, including census and survey reports.

The DHS Program

Demographic and Health Surveys, including several rounds for Tanzania. Free registration is required to download data.

World Bank Open Data

Development indicators for Tanzania and every other country. The WDI package downloads them straight into R.

Humanitarian Data Exchange

Open datasets on Tanzania from humanitarian and development organisations.

A weekly round-up of R news, tutorials and packages.

title: Your first steps in R: from numbers to a chart
text: This tutorial is for people who have never used R before. By the end you’ll have written a few lines of code, summarised a small table of data and drawn a chart. It takes about 30 minutes.

title: Your first steps in R: from numbers to a chart
text:
1. Install R and an editor
You need two free programs:

R, the language itself. Download it from CRAN and choose Windows, macOS or Linux.
An editor to write code in. Most beginners use RStudio Desktop. Positron is a newer alternative from the same company.

Install R first, then the editor. Open the editor and find the Console: that’s where you type the code below and press Enter to run it.






TipNo computer, or can’t install software?



Posit Cloud runs RStudio in your web browser. The free plan is enough for this tutorial.

title: Your first steps in R: from numbers to a chart
text:
2. R as a calculator
R can do arithmetic, just like a calculator:

2 + 3

[1] 5

1500 * 12

[1] 18000

(42000 + 38500) / 2

[1] 40250

title: Your first steps in R: from numbers to a chart
text:
3. Saving values with <-
To keep a value for later, give it a name with the arrow <-. Read it as “gets”:

price_per_kg <- 2500      # price of 1 kg of maize flour, in TZS
kilos_sold <- 18

price_per_kg * kilos_sold

[1] 45000


Names can contain letters, numbers, _ and ., but can’t start with a number. Anything after # is a comment: R ignores it, but it helps people reading your code.

title: Your first steps in R: from numbers to a chart
text:
4. Many values at once: vectors
A vector holds several values of the same kind. Create one with c(), which stands for “combine”. Here are a week of maize flour sales from a small duka (shop), Monday to Sunday:

maize_sales <- c(42000, 38500, 45000, 40000, 51000, 63000, 57000)

sum(maize_sales)    # total for the week

[1] 336500

mean(maize_sales)   # average per day

[1] 48071.43

max(maize_sales)    # best day

[1] 63000


sum(), mean() and max() are functions: you give them something inside the brackets and they give you an answer back.






Note



The shop and its numbers are made up for this tutorial.

title: Your first steps in R: from numbers to a chart
text:
5. Tables of data: data frames
Real data usually comes as a table, with rows and columns. In R a table is called a data frame. Let’s record a week of sales for three products:

sales <- data.frame(
  day = rep(c("Mon", "Tue", "Wed", "Thu", "Fri", "Sat", "Sun"), times = 3),
  product = rep(c("Maize flour", "Cooking oil", "Sugar"), each = 7),
  amount_tzs = c(
    42000, 38500, 45000, 40000, 51000, 63000, 57000,  # maize flour
    25000, 27500, 24000, 26000, 31000, 39000, 34500,  # cooking oil
    18000, 16500, 19500, 17000, 22000, 28500, 25000   # sugar
  )
)

head(sales)   # show the first six rows

  day     product amount_tzs
1 Mon Maize flour      42000
2 Tue Maize flour      38500
3 Wed Maize flour      45000
4 Thu Maize flour      40000
5 Fri Maize flour      51000
6 Sat Maize flour      63000


rep() repeats values, so we don’t have to type every day and product by hand. In practice you would usually read a table from a file, for example with read.csv("sales.csv").

title: Your first steps in R: from numbers to a chart
text:
6. Add-on packages
Thousands of free packages add extra features to R. Two of the most popular are dplyr, for working with tables, and ggplot2, for charts. Install them once:

install.packages(c("dplyr", "ggplot2"))

Then load them each time you start R:

library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

title: Your first steps in R: from numbers to a chart
text:
7. Summarise the week
With dplyr we can ask: how much did each product earn this week, and which was its best day?

weekly <- sales |>
  group_by(product) |>
  summarise(
    total_tzs = sum(amount_tzs),
    best_day = day[which.max(amount_tzs)]
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(total_tzs))

weekly

# A tibble: 3 × 3
  product     total_tzs best_day
  <chr>           <dbl> <chr>   
1 Maize flour    336500 Sat     
2 Cooking oil    207000 Sat     
3 Sugar          146500 Sat     


Read the |> symbol (the pipe) as “and then”: take sales, and then group it by product, and then summarise each group, and then sort from largest to smallest.
Altogether, the shop took in TZS 690,000 this week, and Saturday was the busiest day for every product.

title: Your first steps in R: from numbers to a chart
text:
8. Your first chart
Finally, let’s draw it. ggplot2 builds a chart in layers, joined with +:

ggplot(weekly, aes(x = total_tzs, y = reorder(product, total_tzs))) +
  geom_col(fill = "#0B6E2E", width = 0.6) +
  geom_text(aes(label = scales::comma(total_tzs)), hjust = -0.15, size = 4) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    labels = scales::label_comma(),
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.15))
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Maize flour brought in the most money this week",
    x = "Total sales (TZS)",
    y = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(
    panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    plot.title.position = "plot"
  )







Figure 1: Total sales per product over one week (made-up data).





Line by line:

ggplot(weekly, aes(...)) chooses the data and what goes on each axis. reorder() sorts the bars by size.
geom_col() draws the bars.
geom_text() writes each total next to its bar.
scale_x_continuous() adds commas to the numbers on the axis.
labs() sets the title and axis labels.
theme_minimal() and theme() give it a clean look.

Try changing the colour "#0B6E2E" or the title, then run the code again.

title: Your first steps in R: from numbers to a chart
text:
What next?
Congratulations, you’ve written your first R code! To keep going:

Work through the free book R for Data Science, the standard next step.
Browse our learning resources, including Tanzanian data sources to practise on.
Join the community and come to a meetup. Bring your questions.

Stuck? Ask in our community channels. Everyone was a beginner once.

title: About us
text:
Tanzanian R Users (Jumuiya ya Watumiaji wa R Tanzania) was founded in 2026 to bring together people across Tanzania who use R, the free and open-source language for statistics, data analysis and visualisation.
R is already used in Tanzanian universities, research institutes, hospitals, government offices and NGOs. Yet many users learn on their own, with few chances to meet peers, find a mentor or see how others solve the same problems. We started this community to change that.

title: About us
text:
Tanzanian R Users (Jumuiya ya Watumiaji wa R Tanzania) was founded in 2026 to bring together people across Tanzania who use R, the free and open-source language for statistics, data analysis and visualisation.
R is already used in Tanzanian universities, research institutes, hospitals, government offices and NGOs. Yet many users learn on their own, with few chances to meet peers, find a mentor or see how others solve the same problems. We started this community to change that.

title: About us
text:
Mission
To build a welcoming, inclusive community where people in Tanzania learn R, share knowledge and use data to address local challenges.

title: About us
text:
Vision
A Tanzania where anyone, in any region and at any level, can find the skills, mentors and peers they need to turn data into insight.

title: About us
text:
What we value

Everyone is welcome

Beginners and experts, students and professionals, from every region and background.

Learning by doing

Practical, hands-on sessions built around real problems and real data.

Open knowledge

We share slides, code and recordings openly so that anyone can learn from them.

Local relevance

We focus on the data and questions that matter in Tanzania.

Respect

Everyone in our spaces follows our Code of Conduct.

title: About us
text:
Part of a global community
R users around the world organise local groups, and we’re proud to join them. If you’d like to see what’s happening beyond Tanzania, have a look at AfricaR, R-Ladies and the R Consortium, which supports R user groups worldwide.

title: About us
text:
Partners and supporters
We’re grateful to the organisations that help us with venues, funding and expertise. Interested in supporting the community? Here’s how.

title: Code of Conduct
text:
Tanzanian R Users is dedicated to providing a welcoming, safe and harassment-free experience for everyone, regardless of gender, gender identity and expression, age, sexual orientation, disability, physical appearance, body size, ethnicity, tribe, nationality, religion, language, level of experience, or field of work.
This Code of Conduct applies to all community spaces: meetups, workshops, online events, our WhatsApp and other chat groups, social media, GitHub and this website. It applies to everyone: members, speakers, volunteers, organisers, sponsors and guests.

title: Code of Conduct
text:
What we expect

Be welcoming and kind. Help newcomers. Every expert was once a beginner, and no question is too basic.
Be respectful. Disagree with ideas, not people. Assume good intentions.
Be inclusive. Use language that others can follow, in English or Kiswahili, and make space for quieter voices.
Give credit. Acknowledge other people’s code, ideas and work.
Look out for each other. If you see someone in distress or being treated badly, check on them or tell an organiser.

title: Code of Conduct
text:
What is not acceptable

Harassment, intimidation or discrimination of any kind.
Offensive comments related to any of the personal characteristics listed above.
Sexual language or imagery, and unwelcome sexual attention or physical contact.
Insults, put-downs, trolling or deliberately disrupting talks and discussions.
Photographing, recording or sharing someone’s personal information without their permission.
Spam, and unsolicited advertising or recruitment in community channels.
Encouraging any of the above.

title: Code of Conduct
text:
Reporting a problem
If you experience or witness behaviour that breaks this Code of Conduct, please tell us as soon as you can:

speak to any organiser in person at an event; or
email TODO-community-email@example.org.

All reports are treated seriously and kept confidential. If a report involves an organiser, that person will not take part in handling it.

title: Code of Conduct
Code of Conduct
text:
Credits
This Code of Conduct draws on the codes of conduct of other open-source and R communities, including the Contributor Covenant and R-Ladies. It may be reused and adapted by other communities.

Karibu! This is the first official meetup of Tanzanian R Users. Whether you use R every day or you’re just curious about it, come and meet the people building an R community in Tanzania.

title: Community Launch Meetup
text:
What to expect

Welcome and introductions. Who we are and why we started this community.
Lightning talks. Three or four short talks (5 minutes each) from members about how they use R. Want to give one?
Open discussion. What should we do in 2027? Workshops, study groups, hackathons, a conference? You decide.
Networking. Chai, conversation and new connections.

title: Community Launch Meetup
text:
Who should come
Everyone is welcome: students, researchers, analysts, developers and complete beginners. You don’t need to bring a laptop.

title: Community Launch Meetup
text:
How to register
Registration is free.  Join our community channels to get the registration link and venue details as soon as they’re confirmed.
Questions? Email us at TODO-community-email@example.org.

title: Get involved
text:
Give a talk
We’d love to hear how you use R, at any level. Every talk is welcome:

Lightning talks (5 minutes): one idea, one package, one trick.
Full talks (20–30 minutes): a project, an analysis or a method.
Workshops (1–3 hours): hands-on teaching.

First-time speakers are especially welcome, and we’ll gladly help you prepare.

title: Karibu! Welcome to the Tanzanian R Users community
section: Why a community for R users in Tanzania?

title: Karibu! Welcome to the Tanzanian R Users community
text:
What we’re planning
Over the coming months we’ll start with:

A launch meetup in Dar es Salaam, also streamed online. See the details.
Regular meetups with short talks from members about how they use R.
Beginner workshops for people who have never written a line of code.
This blog, with tutorials, project write-ups and event recaps written by members. Our first tutorial, Your first steps in R, is already up.

We’ll decide the rest together. Tell us what you’d find most useful.

title: Karibu! Welcome to the Tanzanian R Users community
text:
How you can help

Join our channels so you hear about events first. Find them here.
Offer a lightning talk. Five minutes on anything you’ve done with R. First-time speakers are very welcome.
Write a blog post about a project, a package you love or something you learned the hard way.
Tell a friend, a classmate or a colleague who works with data.

title: Karibu! Welcome to the Tanzanian R Users community
text:
A welcoming space
Everyone who takes part, online or in person, agrees to our Code of Conduct. Conversations can happen in English and Kiswahili, and no question is too basic.
Tuonane hivi karibuni. See you soon!
